source: Bonawitz, van Schijndel, Friel, Schulz (2012) Children balance theories and evidence in exploration, explanation, and learning
finding: Children who held a belief about balance explored the block more when the evidence contradicted that belief than when it confirmed it. Children with no theory showed only a novelty preference.
numbers: Exp 1: 95 children aged 6-7 plus 31 aged 4-5. 60 of the 6-7s balanced consistently (32 Center Theorists, 28 Mass Theorists). Playtime theory x evidence interaction F(1,59)=6.02, p<.05. Center Theorists were younger (81 vs 88 months, p<.0001). Exp 3 replicated the interaction, F(1,60)=8.51, p<.01.
limits: Small cells (about 14-16 per condition). One task family (balance). 35 extra 6-7s were excluded for ambiguous belief classification.
agent_relevance: Evidence that testing effort goes where prior and data clash. For S4 TEST: prefer the test whose outcome could contradict the leading hypothesis over a merely novel test.

source: Bonawitz et al. (2012) explanation and belief revision
finding: Children invoked a hidden auxiliary cause (a magnet) mostly when evidence violated their belief. After surprising evidence about a third changed their prediction. After confirming evidence almost none did.
numbers: Mass Theorists in the Geometric Center condition cited the magnet 71% vs 14% in the Center of Mass condition (Fisher p<.01, N=28). Prediction changes after conflicting evidence: 11 of 30 (37%) vs 1 of 30 (3%) after confirming evidence (Fisher p<.01, N=60). Exp 3 (N=32): magnet explanation 63% vs 13% across conditions (p<.01).
quote: children appeal to the magnet only when beliefs are violated
limits: Blind coders, but kappa was moderate in some cells (authors blame small N). Magnet appeal is a very specific rescue move.
agent_relevance: Two reactions to a surprising result: blame an auxiliary assumption first, revise the hypothesis after repeated conflict. Matches G2 (revise from real output); check auxiliary assumptions before dropping a hypothesis.

source: Bonawitz et al. (2012) boundary: unstable beliefs and the no-theory group
finding: The effect needs a stable belief. Children with inconsistent or absent beliefs behave like novelty seekers regardless of evidence.
numbers: Only 63% of 6-7 year olds balanced consistently on all 3 classification trials. 65% of 4-5 year olds split their responses across trials. No Theory group (n=31) preferred the novel toy, F(1,29)=9.43, p<.01, with no condition effect.
limits: Museum sample. Narrow age range.
agent_relevance: Prior-weighted testing only makes sense once a committed hypothesis exists. Before that, broad sampling is the better policy.

source: Gopnik & Wellman (2012) Reconstructing constructivism: causal models, Bayesian learning mechanisms and the theory theory
finding: Main review of the claim that children learn like Bayesian scientists. Reports that children's guesses follow the chip proportions in a bag (probability matching) and go beyond simple reinforcement-learning matching.
numbers: In an 80 red / 20 blue bag a sampler says red 80% of the time; the review says children do this and adjust for a 60/40 bag. 4-year-olds searched for hidden causes when a machine fired only 2 of 6 times (Schulz & Somerville 2006).
limits: Review by the theory's proponents. It reports no failed replications. The authors note that how hypotheses are generated stays open.
agent_relevance: A sampling view (guess in proportion to belief) fits generating several candidate hypotheses and then testing them, not committing to the single most probable one.

source: Gopnik, Griffiths, Lucas et al. (2017) Changes in cognitive flexibility and hypothesis search across human life history (PNAS)
finding: Younger children accept an unlikely causal rule (conjunctive: several blocks needed) from evidence more readily than older children, adolescents and adults. Adults keep the default disjunctive rule.
numbers: Conjunctive condition, share calling the ambiguous object D a blicket: 4-year-olds 0.92, 6-7s 0.56, 9-11s 0.60, 12-14s 0.28, adults 0.25 (Fisher 4 vs 6-7, P<.01; 6-7 vs 12-14, P<.05). Using multiple objects to activate: 4-year-olds 0.84 vs 6-7s 0.53 (P<.05). New samples: 90 (6-7), 90 (9-11), 86 (12-14); the 4-year-old and adult data came from Lucas et al. 2014.
limits: Cross-sectional. Adults had no control over the evidence (see b18). Part of the data was reused from an earlier study, not collected together.
agent_relevance: Prior strength rises with experience and blocks updating. A strong LM prior may act like adult experience: the scaffold needs a step that reopens low-prior hypotheses.

source: Gopnik et al. (2017) Experiment 2: social causality (trait vs situation attribution)
finding: The pattern did not repeat simply in the social domain. Adolescents overcorrected: in the situation condition they were less trait-biased than 6-year-olds and adults (inverted U).
numbers: Baseline situation attributions: 4-year-olds 0.93 vs 12-14-year-olds 0.24 and adults 0.38.
limits: Domain-dependent. Different measure (0-2 score).
agent_relevance: Flexibility is not one dial. A fix for a physical-rule bias will not carry over automatically to social attribution, so test the scaffold per domain.

source: Variability in 2- to 5-year-olds' causal inference behavior (PLoS ONE 2018; authors not read from source)
finding: Partial replication of screening-off and backwards-blocking trials. Success rates matched earlier studies on most matched trials, but children split into three response strategies, not one common Bayesian profile.
numbers: N=90 (23 two-year-olds, 23 three-year-olds, 23 four-year-olds, 21 five-year-olds). Latent class model: Strategy 1 (N=51, mostly older) succeeded on nearly all trials; Strategy 2 (most 2-year-olds) succeeded at .48 on screening-off, .33 on indirect screening-off A, and 0 on backwards blocking; Strategy 3 a small group. Non-causal association trial: 2% succeeded vs 27% in Nazzi & Gopnik 2003.
limits: Exploratory latent class analysis. Authors say associative models could also explain the high-success profile. One comparison with earlier studies differed, which the authors put down to procedure.
agent_relevance: Averages hide a mixture of strategies. Report per-strategy results when judging whether a test policy is Bayesian.

source: Weisberg, Choi, Sobel (2020) Of blickets, butterflies, and baby dinosaurs: children's diagnostic reasoning across domains
finding: Replicated Sobel et al. 2017 with larger samples: 4- to 10-year-olds improve with age at a blicket diagnostic inference, but performance is modest and a same-structure butterfly problem is not easier.
numbers: Exp 1 N=242. Percent correct blicket / butterfly: youngest third 38.5 / 26.2, middle 41.0 / 38.1, oldest 55.3 / 59.5 (chance about 33%). Exp 2 N=103 within subject: 46% blicket, 42% butterfly, both above chance (p=.005, p=.04); identical to Exp 1. Only 38% (blicket) vs 24% (butterfly) tried the correct pair first, chi2(1, N=214)=5.20, p=.02. 82% saw the tasks as similar, but 70% cited perceptual not causal similarity.
limits: Only 39 blicket children gave justifications in Exp 1. Chance level is a three-way guess rate.
agent_relevance: Even the classic task is hard and structure does not transfer unless re-represented. State the causal structure explicitly before reuse.

source: Kosoy, Chan, Liu et al. (2022) Towards understanding how machines can learn causal overhypotheses
finding: Benchmark of deep RL, behavior cloning, decision transformer and two LLMs on blicket overhypotheses. Models struggled where children succeed from a handful of observations.
numbers: Decision transformer: reward 0.16 (random data) vs 2.06 (random with 5-step forced exploration), forced choice accuracy 0.67 vs 0.71. Behavior cloning reward 0.04-0.12, FCA 0.59-0.68. GPT-3 (text-davinci-002) and PaLM almost always chose the correct structure when hypotheses were given, but GPT-3 named too many blickets. With hypotheses not given they could not express uncertainty. Chain-of-thought did not help PaLM.
limits: Tiny LM test set (a few prompts per cell). 2022 models.
agent_relevance: A defined hypothesis space lets an LM reason about structure. Give the agent an explicit list of candidate hypotheses before S4, not an open question.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (PNAS)
finding: GPT-3 passed a simple blicket vignette and some causal vignettes but failed a seeing-versus-doing task in the causal-chain condition, which suggests surface pattern use.
numbers: Blicket vignette: first object a blicket, second not (correct). Twelve vignette problems: 6 answered correctly. Waldmann-Hagmayer seeing/doing: correct in common cause; in causal chain it gave identical predictions to common cause; after observing B=0 it did not lower its prediction.
limits: text-davinci-002 only. Authors warn the vignettes may be in the training set.
agent_relevance: Passing a famous vignette is weak evidence. Use fresh or re-skinned structures (G3).

source: Jin et al. (2024) Can large language models infer causation from correlation? Corr2Cause (ICLR 2024)
finding: Pure causal inference from correlation statements is very hard for LLMs. 17 models were near or below chance. Fine-tuned models score high but collapse under paraphrase and renamed variables.
numbers: 207,972 samples, 18.57% positive. Best F1 33.38 (BART MNLI), higher than GPT-4; random uniform F1 20.38. Many models worse than random. Fine-tuned RoBERTa-Large MNLI F1 94.74, but dropped by up to 39.29 F1 on paraphrases and up to 62.30 on variable refactorization (best model kept 67.87 on refactorization). Few-shot chain-of-thought did not rescue it.
limits: Formal d-separation style task. Fine-tuning gains reflect distribution fitting, not skill.
agent_relevance: Do not ask the LM to infer causal structure from correlations alone. Use code (a conditional-independence check) or an intervention (S4 test).

source: Jin et al. (2023) CLadder: assessing causal reasoning in language models
finding: 10K questions across association, intervention and counterfactual, with oracle answers. GPT-4 about 62% to 64%. A structured chain-of-thought (CausalCoT) gave a gain.
numbers: CausalCoT 70.40%, +8.37 over vanilla GPT-4 (gpt-4-1106-preview). Earlier May 2023 GPT-4 run 63.95%; its CausalCoT 66.64% (+2.36). GPT-4 5.34 points worse on nonsensical variable names than on commonsensical ones.
limits: Template-generated questions. Per-slice values read from text extraction.
agent_relevance: Stepwise causal prompts (graph, query type, formula, compute) help by a few points. Do the arithmetic in code.

source: Kiciman, Ness, Sharma, Tan (2024) Causal reasoning and large language models: opening a new frontier for causality
finding: LLMs generate correct causal arguments from text metadata at high rates but fail unpredictably and cannot use the data itself.
numbers: Abstract figures: pairwise causal discovery 97% (13-point gain over prior best), counterfactual reasoning 92% (20-point gain), event causality 86% for necessary and sufficient causes. Robustness checks on datasets created after the training cutoff.
limits: I read the abstract and framing only, not each table. Variable names carry meaning, so stored knowledge may explain the gain. Contrasts with Corr2Cause (b11).
agent_relevance: Use the LM to propose causal graphs from domain knowledge, then check with data or intervention.

source: Qiu, Sha, Allen, Kim, Linzen, van Steenkiste (2026) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in LLMs
finding: Off-the-shelf LLMs do not update beliefs like a Bayesian assistant over repeated rounds. Fine-tuning on the Bayesian model's predictions closes much of the gap and transfers to new domains.
numbers: Flight recommendation, 624 simulated users, 5 rounds. Bayesian Assistant 81% final-round accuracy; off-the-shelf LLMs about 36-58% (read from figure text), with little gain after round 1. Humans (48 users) improved (p=0.002) but stayed below Bayes. Bayesian-tuned LLMs agree with the Bayesian model about 80% of the time; oracle-tuned models are worse and vary more. Chain-of-thought, numeric formats and 30 rounds did not meaningfully help.
limits: Training-based fix; we do not train. Simple preference task, not causal. Values read from figure text.
agent_relevance: Keep posteriors in code. Prompting (including chain-of-thought) did not make LLMs update. Supports G5.

source: GX-Chen, Lin, Samiei, Precup, Richards, Fergus, Marino (2025) Language agents mirror human causal reasoning biases (COLM 2025)
finding: LM agents (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1, Gemma3, QwQ, Llama) infer disjunctive blicket rules well but fail conjunctive ones: a disjunctive bias like human adults, not children.
numbers: InfoGain Oracle accuracy 1.0 everywhere. LMs worse at 8 than 4 objects and worse for AND than OR. Information gain correlated with final accuracy (Spearman about 0.76); response length correlated negatively (about -0.30, p<.05). Some frontier models explored no better than random. Even with oracle exploration data LMs were not near perfect.
limits: Spearman values read from a plotted panel. Text interface. Early-2025 models.
agent_relevance: Conjunctive and unusual hypotheses must be put into the candidate set by construction.

source: GX-Chen et al. (2025) hypothesis-sampling agent: flattening the LM prior at test time
finding: Sample many distinct hypotheses as Python functions, give equal weight, choose the action that eliminates the most, repeat. This removed the disjunctive bias and improved exploration.
numbers: Initial unique hypotheses 16, 32, 64, 96: Q&A accuracy and exploration improved with more samples; with enough samples no conjunctive vs disjunctive gap in the 8-object environment.
limits: One environment. Effect depends on how many unique hypotheses are sampled. More calls.
agent_relevance: Directly usable in S4: enumerate hypotheses as executable predicates, weight uniformly, pick the test that eliminates most. Code selects (G5).

source: GX-Chen et al. (2025) LM versus child and adult inference profiles
finding: LM agents matched adult-like, not 4-year-old, rates of calling the ambiguous key object a blicket after conjunctive evidence. Effort and exploration also differed from children.
numbers: Human data replicated from Gopnik et al. 2017; child exploration from Table 1 of Kosoy et al. 2022. LMs adjusted exploration more by rule type than children did.
limits: Child data are secondary.
agent_relevance: Do not assume LM exploration is child-like. Add forced breadth for high stakes.

source: Samiei, Yiu, GX-Chen et al. (2026) Human adults and LLMs as scientists: who benefits from active exploration?
finding: Adults' conjunctive handicap largely disappears when they choose their own tests. Proposing tests that someone else runs gives no benefit. Some LLMs approach human accuracy but explore less efficiently.
numbers: 306 adults. Conjunctive object identification: Active Explorer 0.69, Passive Observer 0.45, Passive Proposer 0.12; rule selection 0.82, 0.69, 0.57. Tests used: 9.6 (conjunctive) vs 6.4 (disjunctive) for average humans. gpt-5 10.2 vs 7.7 tests; gemini-2.5-flash 13.5 vs 9.7. gpt-5 and deepseek-reasoner near-perfect; models: gpt-5, gpt-5-mini, gemini-2.5-flash, deepseek-reasoner, o4-mini.
limits: Preprint (June 2026), not peer reviewed. New 'nexiom' task with 4 objects. Online adults.
agent_relevance: Key for S4: the same agent should choose the test and see its own result before updating. Tests chosen by someone else and merely observed did not help.

source: Samiei et al. (2026) accuracy by age group
finding: Rule-inference accuracy by age (6-7, 9-11, 12-14, adults) for conjunctive and disjunctive rules in the active task; conjunctive accuracy rises with age.
numbers: Approximate values from figure text: conjunctive about 0.28 for 6-7 years up to about 0.86-0.96 for adults; disjunctive 0.86-0.96 across ages.
limits: Figure values read from text extraction without bars; treat as approximate.
agent_relevance: Ceiling for conjunctive learning is high when the learner acts.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to falsify: confirmation bias in language models
finding: Eleven LLMs show confirmation bias in a Wason 2-4-6 style rule discovery game: they propose triples that fit their current guess. This links to lower success.
numbers: Task success 6% to 78% within a 45-turn limit across eleven models. Reasoning models do better and are less biased. Success correlates negatively with confirmation bias. A falsification instruction raised rule discovery from 42% to 56% on average.
limits: Number triples. Success depends on the turn limit. Prompt effect is an average over models.
agent_relevance: Supports G3 and an explicit step: seek a test the current hypothesis forbids.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) transfer to the blicket test (Think-in-Opposites, TiO)
finding: A falsification prompt (TiO) raised success and the incompatible-to-compatible test ratio on thinking models in the blicket task. Distilling the behavior from the Wason task transferred partly.
numbers: 192 episodes per cell (2x2x3x16). Success and I:C ratio correlated positively for thinking and non-thinking models. Qwen3-8B success 0.32 -> 0.40 with TiO (I:C 0.44 -> 0.57). Same-scale distillation (8B, 32B) improved over base but stayed below direct TiO prompting. Effects for non-thinking models were substantially smaller.
limits: Some models did not improve (Qwen3-14B non-thinking 0.25 vs 0.20). Table columns read from text extraction.
agent_relevance: Helps mainly strong reasoning models. Measure per backend.

source: Jiang & Lucas (2024) Actively learning to learn causal relationships (Computational Brain & Behavior)
finding: Two preregistered active blicket studies. A hierarchical Bayesian model that values information about overhypotheses predicted most individuals best, but a simpler no-transfer model won at group level.
numbers: Exp 1 N=212 (181 after filtering). Exp 2 N=250, 20 interventions each, 6 blocks. Mean predictive likelihood: No-Transfer .059 (SE .002), full model .055 (.003), Fixed-Form .018, Structure-Only-EIG .018, random .016. 81.63% of fits weighted overhypothesis information gain over structure; 45.41% put all weight on it.
limits: Exp 1 found no significant gain on the hard conjunctive transfer task. Parameters (temperature, weight) were fitted.
agent_relevance: People learn how causes combine, but not everyone does. An optional memory of rule forms across tasks may help; check on held-out tasks.

source: Jiang & Lucas (2024) boundary: transfer and positive testing
finding: Many adults treated each task as new and tested one block at a time as if a single cause were enough. This positive-testing habit hides conjunctive rules.
numbers: The No-Transfer ablation captured the second-largest group of individuals. The Fixed-Form (disjunctive-only) model was best for no one in the conjunctive training condition.
limits: Inferred from model fits. Short online tasks.
agent_relevance: Test combinations, not only single items, when the effect might need more than one cause.

source: Yiu, Kosoy, Gopnik (2024) Transmission versus truth, imitation versus innovation (Perspectives on Psychological Science)
finding: LLMs imitate familiar associations well but are weaker at inventing new tool uses. GPT-4 is best of the models but below adults.
numbers: Children 3-7 (n=42): 88.4% associate, 85.2% innovate. Adults (n=30): 84.9% and 95.7%. LLM imitation / innovation: GPT-4 83.3% / 75.9%; gpt-3.5-turbo 73.1% / 58.9%; text-davinci 59.9% / 8.87%; Claude 69.9% / 58.2%. Six option orders each, temperature 0. Models sometimes cited the authors' own blicket papers.
limits: Contamination risk for the blicket task. GPT-4's gain could come from RLHF or multimodality (open).
agent_relevance: Famous developmental tasks leak into training data. Test on re-skinned or new structures.

source: Is the Bayesian brain a myth? (2025, Eur J Appl Physiol) summarising Bowers & Davis (2012)
finding: A 2025 critique argues Bayesian models are too flexible to be falsified, with priors adjusted after the fact, and that the as-if defence avoids mechanism.
numbers: Qualitative. A table lists responses to contradiction: adjust priors to fit data, invoke suboptimal inference, retreat to as-if. Cites Bowers & Davis 2012 on post hoc parameters.
limits: Opinion piece, not an empirical test. I did not open Bowers & Davis or Jones & Love directly.
agent_relevance: Treat Bayesian fits as a design aid, not proof. Judge the scaffold by held-out test outcomes.

source: Sobel, Tenenbaum, Gopnik (2004) Children's causal inferences from indirect evidence: backwards blocking and Bayesian reasoning in preschoolers (Cognitive Science)
finding: Founding backwards-blocking study. Not opened. The 2018 PLoS replication (b07) found matching success on indirect screening-off and backwards blocking for 3-year-olds but a mixture of strategies.
numbers: Not recorded from the source. See b07.
limits: Others claim associative models fit the same data (as cited in b07).
agent_relevance: The core pattern replicates; the Bayesian reading is not settled.

source: Lucas, Bridgers, Griffiths, Gopnik (2014) When children are better (or at least more open-minded) learners than adults (Cognition)
finding: Preschoolers inferred an unusual conjunctive rule from evidence while adults stayed with the disjunctive default. Known only via b05 and b15.
numbers: Three experiments in the original; numbers not opened here. Its 4-year-old and adult data are reused in b05.
limits: Not read directly. b18 shows the adult gap shrinks when adults act.
agent_relevance: The adult-like bias in LMs is a documented human bias.
